region: Mountain and northern forests of Europe, Asia, North Africa and North America
description: True firs give a pale, light, fairly soft wood that is sold mixed with spruce and pine as framing and general construction lumber, and used for joinery, crates and plywood. It is not the same tree as Douglas fir.

hazards.summary: A review of wood allergy lists fir (Abies) among woods reported to cause occupational asthma, based on German studies of wood workers. We could not access those original studies, so this remains a reported, unconfirmed link.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses. This applies to this wood like every other species.

related_species_note: Fir is usually sold and processed together with spruce and pine; reports of softwood allergy may involve more than one of these.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed European silver fir (Abies alba) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Pale creamy white to light buff wood, sometimes with a faint greyish or pinkish tinge, with no clear distinction between heartwood and sapwood. Straight grain with clearly defined growth rings where the latewood bands are slightly darker, a medium-fine even texture, low luster and no resin canals or visible pores. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of fir with pale creamy wood and straight, evenly spaced growth rings.
notes_internal: Genus entry; image uses Abies alba. Schlunssen-2018 Table 1 cites Kersten 1994 (Allergologie 17:55-60) and Kespohl 2011/2012 for fir OA. Kespohl-2012 abstract names spruce, pine and larch only, so it was not cited for fir. Kersten 1994 not reachable (German journal, no PubMed). Fir is not listed in HSE-WIS30. Evidence level 3 via Tier B per brief.
